Content:
Consider the following equations of a line [MATH: l] and a plane [MATH: \Pi\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: l: \mathbf{r} = \langle 2,2,1 \rangle + t \langle 3,0,1 \rangle, \qquad \Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 3,-5,1 \rangle = 7.]
How can we find the intersection point [MATH: P] of [MATH: l] and [MATH: \Pi?]

Content:
We start by writing the equation of the line in the form [MATH: \mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle.] Now, since [MATH: P] must lie on the line [MATH: l,] we can write its coordinates as [MATH: P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)] for some particular value of [MATH: t \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c99c9eb2443a6887cdf10542c90639a0]

Content:
On the other hand, [MATH: P] also lies on the plane [MATH: \Pi.] So, the coordinates [MATH: P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)] must satisfy the equation of the plane as well. Substituting the position vector [MATH: \mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle] into the equation of the plane and solving for [MATH: t,] we get
[MATH: r ⋅ ⟨3, − 5, 1⟩|= 7; ⟨2 + 3t, 2, 1 + t⟩ ⋅ ⟨3, − 5, 1⟩|= 7; 3(2 + 3t) − 5 ⋅ 2 + (1 + t)|= 7; 6 + 9t − 10 + 1 + t|= 7; 10t|= 10; t|= 1.]

Content:
To get the position vector [MATH: \mathbf{p}] of the intersection point [MATH: P,] we substitute [MATH: t=1] into the equation of the line:
[MATH: p|= ⟨2 + 3(1), 2, 1 + (1)⟩; = ⟨5, 2, 2⟩]

Content:
Therefore, the intersection point is [MATH: P(5, 2, 2).]
